title: kv-occupancy-sampling-eviction-horizon-notes
content:
Purpose / motivation:
This note records a set of profiling experiments and design thoughts aimed at improving KV cache behavior under skewed hotsets and variable sequence-length workloads. The focus is on: occupancy sampling (how we estimate residency and hotness), defining an eviction horizon (temporal vs. access-count horizon), and quantifying memory-bandwidth impact of different eviction/prefetch policies.

Quick summary of takeaways (TL;DR):
- Short, high-frequency sampling windows (250ms) capture hot churn better than long windows (5s) in high-concurrency workloads; reuse_rate estimate variance drops ~40%.
- Eviction horizon based on decayed access-score (half-life 800ms) produced fewer cold-evictions and improved P95 latency by ~6% compared to strict LRU in our synthetic chat trace.
- Aggressive prefetch (prefetch-on-evict for predicted-followups) reduced PCIe reads by ~18% on R4 tests, but increased peak memory-bandwidth by ~12% — tradeoff depends on SLO headroom.
- Sampling itself has cost; careful batching of occupancy probes is necessary to keep CPU overhead <3%.

Background / problem statement:
- Observed: intermittent P95 latency spikes under realistic multi-tenant workloads. Root-cause signal points to KV cache thrash and host paging (reads from network/NVMe).
- Hypothesis: our current eviction decisions (approx-LRU with coarse time buckets) under-estimate short-lived bursts and evict blocks that will be re-used within the next 1s, incurring host fetches and amplifying bandwidth usage.

Experiment design:
- Testbed: 2x p4d-like nodes (simulated), serving runtime in standalone mode, model serving QPS generated by replayed traces from production chat (anonymized).
- Key metrics: reuse_rate (fraction of evicted blocks that are re-accessed within 1s), host_fetch_bytes, p95_token_latency, memory_bandwidth_util (sampled by nvidia-smi/pmon), cpu-percent-for-sampling.
- Policies compared:
  1) baseline-lru-coarse: current production (bucketed LRU, 5s bucket refresh)
  2) sample-window-250ms: occupancy sampling every 250ms, update hotness score
  3) decay-score-800ms: use exponential-decay score (lambda tuned for ~800ms half-life) to set eviction horizon
  4) prefetch-predictive: when evict candidate is followed by a predicted dependent key (simple 2-gram from recent sequence), prefetch instead of evict
  5) hybrid: decay-score + predictive-prefetch limited to 10MB/s prefetch budget

Commands / profiling tools used:
- perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 120 (CPU sampling for sampling thread hotspots)
- nvprof --profile-from-start off --log-file nvprof.log 
- custom runtime counters: kv.residency_bytes, kv.evictions_total, kv.prefetch_bytes, kv.sample_probes_total
- scapy-style trace replay: ./replay_trace --rate 1200 --seq-dist=prod-dist.json

Selected results (aggregated, averages across 3 runs):

Table (text):
Policy | reuse_rate(1s) | host_fetch_GB | p95_token_ms | mem_bw_util(%) | cpu_sampling_pct
baseline-lru-coarse | 0.27 | 124.6 | 34.8 | 52 | 1.1
sample-window-250ms | 0.36 | 101.2 | 33.2 | 54 | 2.5
decay-score-800ms | 0.41 | 95.3 | 32.7 | 56 | 2.9
prefetch-predictive | 0.44 | 81.1 | 31.6 | 68 | 3.8
hybrid | 0.43 | 89.7 | 32.1 | 61 | 3.4

Interpretation:
- reuse_rate improvements correlate with reduced host_fetch volume and lower P95. Decay-based horizon performs better than simple sampling alone because it smooths bursty spikes while still valuing recent accesses.
- Prefetching gives the biggest drop in host fetches but increases memory bandwidth usage and slightly increases CPU due to prefetch handling. It also risks polluting cache if prediction precision is low.
- Hybrid strikes a reasonable tradeoff when we cap prefetch budget; it recovers most host_fetch savings without fully doubling memory bandwidth.

Micro-profiling notes (hotspots):
- Sampling thread: 40% cycles spent in lock acquisition when naive per-key locks were used. Switched to per-shard sampling buffer and lock-free append reduced contention.
- Eviction walker: memory walk accounted for ~12% CPU; avoid scanning whole slab by maintaining small candidate ring per-shard.
- Prefetch path: DMA submission latency (NVMe/PCIe) and queueing visible; we need backpressure so prefetches don't overload the device.

Observed anomalies / surprising behaviours:
- For read-heavy short-seq traces (average seq len < 64 tokens) coarse LRU performed almost as well as decay-score; hypothesis: small sequences have predictable reuse patterns and coarse buckets suffice.
- For mixed workloads with long sequences, we saw a pathological case where predictive-prefetch increased P99 by 9% due to cache pollution when predictions were mis-ranked under new prompt templates.

Implementation details / sketch for decay-score eviction:
- Maintain per-key score S updated on access: S = S * exp(-dt / tau) + 1.0, where dt is time since last update; tau tuned to 1154ms for half-life ~800ms.
- Eviction chooses lowest S candidate from per-shard ring; on ties prefer oldest-last-access to avoid starvation.
- Sampling optimization: instead of updating S on every token, maintain a lightweight per-request list of touched keys and apply batched decay updates at end of request to reduce atomic ops.

Experiment checklist / TODOs:
- [ ] Run longer 24-hour soak for hybrid policy under multi-tenant churn to detect slow regressions.
- [ ] Add adversarial synthetic traces (zipf with exponent 1.3 and bursty arrivals) to stress eviction horizon decisions.
- [ ] Instrument GPU memory-bandwidth per-process (nsight) to correlate prefetch bursts with model stalls.
- [ ] Add A/B rollout plan for canary in Dedicated pool (limit to 5% of traffic), include automatic fallback to baseline-lru when host_fetch_rate spikes > 20% over baseline.

Open questions / discussion items:
- What is our acceptable increase in average memory bandwidth to achieve X% reduction in host fetches? (business/infra tradeoff)
- Should we expose prefetch budget as a per-tenant config or keep global to simplify safety?
- Is eviction-decision latency (ms) acceptable for the decay-score approach at 10K QPS per shard? We need microbench numbers after lock optimizations.

Notes to self / quick ideas:
- Explore tiny Bloom for short-term follow-ups: instead of prefetching whole block, prefetch only header/meta and lazily fetch remainder on first use. Might reduce PCIe reads and still lower tail.
- Consider combining decay-score with an age-based penalty for very large KV blocks to prevent large-block thrash.

Relevant tickets / next commits:
- ENG-1023: add per-shard decay-score + candidate ring (work in progress)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487 - initial sampling refactor (contains perf counters used above)
- CONFLUENCE-8402: arch-level notes on prefetch safety and SLO impact
